item.title: The LR2 Lifetime Distribution: Rate Crossing, Reliability Properties, and Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.18902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the LR2 one-parameter lifetime distribution obtained by mixing an exponential component of rate $\theta/2$ and a gamma component with shape four and rate $\theta^2$. The exponential mixing probability is $\theta^2/(1+\theta^2)$ for $\theta>0$. We derive the density, survival function, moments, transforms, truncated moments, quantiles, order-statistic distributions, mean residual life, and stress--strength reliability. Identifiability follows from the density at the origin, and strict monotonicity of the mean yields a unique moment estimator. A complete density-turning-point criterion and analytic initial and tail hazard expansions clarify the possible shapes. The component rates cross at one half. The hazard decreases initially for every positive parameter and eventually increases in the gamma-dominated regime; it eventually decreases in the exponential-dominated regime. We develop likelihood estimation, observed information, constrained expectation--maximization, spacing estimation, and inference under regularity conditions, and state the likelihood for independent right censoring. A reproducible Monte Carlo study with eight settings and 4,000 generated samples compares likelihood and moment estimation and evaluates log-scale confidence intervals. The analysis distinguishes mathematical properties from empirical validation and explains the restrictions associated with a fixed working time unit.
item.dc:creator: Lalita Singh

item.title: Linear regression with probabilistic networks for network-linked data
item.description: arXiv:2610.18937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network-linked data combine a network with covariates and responses observed for its nodes. Common regression approaches either model dependence among neighboring responses using the observed network or capture similarities associated with network structure without explicitly modeling response dependence. We propose a probabilistic network-linked data analysis framework that incorporates both features while accounting for randomness in network formation. The model uses normalized connection probabilities to weight peer responses and latent positions to capture network cohesion. A two-step likelihood procedure first estimates the network structure and then fits the response model. We establish theoretical guarantees for network recovery in sparse networks with heterogeneous node effects, and prove consistency and joint asymptotic normality of the regression estimators subject to suitable conditions. The analysis also clarifies when estimating the network preserves the classical convergence rate for spatial autoregressive models. Simulation studies demonstrate the estimation performance of the method and assess its inference accuracy. An analysis of diplomatic network data illustrates its practical application.
item.dc:creator: Jingnan Zhang, Shiwen Ye, Danyang Huang

item.title: Subdata Selection for Measurement-Constrained Linear Regression under Model Misspecification
item.description: arXiv:2610.19351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many modern applications, obtaining response variables is costly, time-consuming, or technically challenging, making it impractical to measure outcomes for all available units. In such settings, covariates may be available for a large pool of candidates, but responses can only be collected for a small, carefully selected subset, making the choice of which units to measure a consequential decision. Most existing subsampling methods are developed for massive datasets, emphasizing the trade-off between statistical accuracy and computational cost, and typically relying on the assumption of a correctly specified model. These features limit their suitability in measurement-constrained settings, where statistical efficiency is paramount and model misspecification is often unavoidable. To address these challenges, we develop a new subset selection framework for linear regression that accommodates potential model misspecification. The proposed approach targets predictive expected loss and yields an A-optimality-type criterion that depends only on covariate information, requiring no response observations at the selection stage. We refer to this method as Expected Loss Optimal Selection (ELOS). By focusing on predictive risk rather than model-based optimality, ELOS remains well-defined and robust under misspecification. Simulation studies and real data applications demonstrate that ELOS achieves strong predictive performance and compares favorably with existing methods across a range of scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Yundi Kong, Min Yang, Ping-Shou Zhong

item.title: Longitudinal Brain Aging in Covariance Space: Temporally Calibrated Bayesian Inference for Adaptive Covariance Operators
item.description: arXiv:2610.19353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Functional brain aging is often characterized by differences between people of different ages, although aging unfolds within individuals. This distinction is especially important for functional connectivity, where the direction of covariance change may evolve across adulthood. We introduce a Bayesian longitudinal covariance-operator framework that models each visit covariance as a latent positive-definite state informed by repeated resting-state fMRI runs. The approach calibrates run-level information for temporal dependence and replicate variability, separates within-person aging from between-person age differences, and uses an adaptive tangent representation to learn the low-dimensional structure of longitudinal change without relying on pooled covariance variation. The longitudinal operator varies smoothly in magnitude and orientation with age, while exact Fr\'echet derivatives translate the fitted trajectory to the covariance scale. This framework allows us to examine how brain covariance organization changes within individuals, whether longitudinal aging follows the population age gradient, and which functional systems contribute to their divergence. In the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study, within-person covariance aging differs substantially from the cross-sectional age gradient through early and middle adulthood, with the discrepancy diminishing later in life. Covariance reorganization is strongest around midlife, and the longitudinal signal is concentrated in a few coordinated directions, with most off-diagonal change occurring between functional systems. These findings demonstrate that population-level signatures of brain aging do not necessarily reflect individual aging trajectories and highlight the importance of modeling longitudinal covariance change directly.
item.dc:creator: Montserrat Fuentes, Yi Zhao

item.title: Common Signals, Spurious Cross-Excitation, and Identification in Multivariate Hawkes Processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.19428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multivariate Hawkes models are widely used to measure endogenous interactions in event data, but latent common signals can generate apparent excitation even without structural interaction. We characterize the resulting linear projection and construct stable, nonnegative Hawkes processes that share the mean intensity and Bartlett spectrum of common-signal models despite having different excitation mechanisms. This establishes a concrete form of second-order non-identification. We derive integrated third-order cumulants for Hawkes processes with Cox immigration and establish generic local identification of normalized structural parameters in two- and three-dimensional systems. An exact-equivalence Monte Carlo experiment demonstrates how third-order information can distinguish mechanisms with identical second-order structure, while revealing substantial finite-sample limitations under weak signals. For a restricted parametric family, we develop Whittle estimation from binned counts, establish consistency and asymptotic normality under appropriate identification conditions, and construct feasible sandwich standard errors accounting for estimated mean intensities. Simulations assess structural recovery and inference accuracy. An application to cryptocurrency transactions illustrates the sensitivity of inferred excitation to model specification and the limitations of structural interpretation based on spectral fit alone.
item.dc:creator: Jiwon Jung, Kiseop Lee

item.title: Model-Induced Hazard Geometry and Functional Representations in Survival Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.19643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Individualized survival predictions are often summarized by scalar risk scores or event probabilities at selected time horizons, although clinically relevant risk may also differ in its temporal organization. We consider finite-dimensional representations of individual hazard trajectories through interpretable hazard functionals, such as peak timing, cumulative hazard over prespecified intervals, and persistence of elevated risk. A central issue is that the richness of such representations is constrained by the hazard geometry supported by the underlying survival model. We formalize this through model-induced tangent spaces and functional ranks, derive an exact decomposition of model-supported variation into directions retained and lost by a chosen representation, and introduce a model-relative notion of local completeness. We further distinguish intrinsic model capacity from the variation actually activated by covariates. These results motivate a structured extension of AFT time scaling through a positive-affine deformation on the log-time scale, yielding a power-warp mechanism with an additional temporal deformation direction. Combined with a log-logistic reference hazard, this gives a parsimonious likelihood-based working specification for which peak timing and peak height provide complete coordinates over the unimodal regime. We also establish plug-in recovery and asymptotic inference for hazard functionals. Simulations and a lung-cancer application illustrate how model-induced restrictions propagate to hazard-functional representations.
item.dc:creator: Xijia Liu

item.title: Generalized Odds for Ordinal Outcomes: A Causal Inference Framework Adjusting for Covariates
item.description: arXiv:2610.19747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Generalized Odds (Gen Odds) provide summaries for ordinal outcomes without requiring the proportional odds assumption. However, conventional Gen Odds compares independently drawn treatment and control outcomes and targets a population-level contrast rather than an individual-level contrast. We developed an individual-level causal formulation of Gen Odds and examined its identification. Methods: We defined the Causal Gen Odds using the joint distribution of potential outcomes and identified it under conditional independence of the potential outcomes given baseline covariates. We developed a model-based estimator using nonproportional cumulative logistic regression and introduced an odds-ratio sensitivity parameter to assess departures from conditional independence. We evaluated the estimators through simulations and illustrated them using data from the ACCORD Study. Results: In simulations, the conditional-independence estimator was approximately unbiased with 95.5% confidence interval coverage under conditional independence, but bias and undercoverage increased with residual dependence. When the sensitivity-analysis estimator incorporated the data-generating dependence parameter, bias remained below 0.01 and coverage ranged from 93.7% to 96.1% across examined settings. In the ACCORD Study, the Causal Gen Odds for right-foot pre-tibial edema was 0.909 (95% CI: 0.880 to 0.940) under conditional independence and remained stable across the examined sensitivity range. Conclusions: The Causal Gen Odds provides an individual-level estimand that complements the conventional population-level Gen Odds. This framework enables estimation of this contrast while explicitly assessing its robustness to assumptions about dependence between potential outcomes.
item.dc:creator: Runnian Huang, Dandan Shi, Lan Liu, Yunjian Yin

item.title: Principal Component Analysis for Zero-Inflated Probability Measures via Lorenz Curves
item.description: arXiv:2610.19874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a principal component analysis framework for probability measures associated with non-negative real-valued random variables with structural zeros. Specifically, leveraging the associated Lorenz Curve (LC) and a suitable perspective transformation of the plane, a bijective embedding is defined to treat such measures as functional data in a Hilbert space. Once the random LC is embedded in this space, standard Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) becomes directly applicable, and the diffeomorphic nature of the embedding allows the main convergence results and their interpretations to be transferred back to the original space of LC. The a.s. and $L^2(\mathbb{P})$ consistency of the estimated eigenfunctions, eigenvalues, and modes of variation is subsequently investigated, both in the embedded space and, by virtue of the embedding's diffeomorphism property, in the original LC space. Crucially, this consistency analysis accounts for the double stochasticity of the estimation problem: one level of randomness is tied to the underlying LC process itself, while the other stems from the empirical estimation of the LC from sample data. As a consequence, consistency of the Karhunen--Lo\`eve reconstructions is also established, guaranteeing faithful approximation of individual curves in both spaces. Finally, the proposed FPCA methodology is illustrated on a real-world dataset of global export flows and compared with a naive FPCA approach.
item.dc:creator: Giacomo Aletti, Enea G. Bongiorno

item.title: Interactive and Robust PCA Graphics with FSDA in MATLAB
item.description: arXiv:2610.19886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a standard method for dimension reduction and the exploratory analysis of multivariate data, but a complete applied workflow often requires more than numerical eigenvectors and static plots. This article documents a set of routines in the FSDA toolbox for MATLAB that implements an integrated workflow for interactive and robust PCA graphics. The software contribution consists of coordinating classical SVD-based PCA, dynamic biplot scaling controlled by row and column parameters, score-distance and orthogonal-distance diagnostics, hard-trimming robust PCA through the Minimum Covariance Determinant and the Forward Search, linked brushing, geographical displays, and three-dimensional projection diagnostics. The implementation returns reproducible numerical output while also exposing graphical controls for changing biplot geometry, confidence regions, displayed labels, robust trimming levels, and linked selections. The methodology is illustrated on quality-of-life indicators for Italian provinces, where the software reveals variable groups, atypical provinces, robust and non-robust PCA structures, and geographical patterns. The emphasis is on statistical software: no new PCA estimator is proposed, but established PCA and robust-PCA methodology is combined in a documented, extensible, and script-reproducible MATLAB environment.
item.dc:creator: Marco Riani, Anthony C. Atkinson, Aldo Corbellini, Domenico Perrotta, Francesca Torti, Gianluca Morelli

item.title: Improved Forecasting for Multivariate Time Series using GNAR models with General Inverse Distance Weights
item.description: arXiv:2610.19921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many multivariate time series arise on networks where relationships between variables depend on physical or more general distances. Standard vector autoregressive models struggle in such settings due to their quadratic parameter growth, while generalised network autoregressive (GNAR) models offer a parsimonious alternative by explicitly incorporating network structures. Existing GNAR formulations assume fixed weights, typically uniform or reciprocal distances, which may not reflect the true influence of distance in real systems. We introduce a novel model with general inverse distance weights (GNARID) that extends GNAR by introducing a tunable exponent parameter that controls the strength of distance penalisation. We establish theoretical results on the consistency and asymptotic normality of new GNARID estimators, including an extension to the setting where the number of nodes grows. We analyse the effect of misspecifying the exponent on forecasting error, which helps assess how much GNAR models could be improved by our tunable weights. Simulation studies confirm the theoretical properties and show measurable benefits from correct weight specification. Using the Brumadinho ground displacement dataset, we show that proper tuning of the weight exponent improves predictive performance, highlighting the practical value of flexible distance-based weighting in network time series models.
item.dc:creator: Hengxu Liu, Guy P. Nason, Sourav Das, Stephen Grebby

item.title: Testing for Peer Effects in Heteroskedastic Fixed-Effects Panels
item.description: arXiv:2610.20045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study testing for peer effects in linear panel models with individual and time fixed effects when the interaction network is unspecified. We propose a quadratic-form test based on the Gram matrix of residualized peer covariates. A key difficulty is that fixed-effects removal and nuisance estimation destroy the centering of a conventional leave-diagonal-out quadratic form under conditional heteroskedasticity. We introduce a leverage adjustment that restores exact conditional centering and combine it with a residual-based variance estimator. The resulting studentized statistic is asymptotically standard normal as both panel dimensions diverge, without imposing any restriction on their relative growth rates. Under additional conditions, we establish consistency against alternatives. The null theory is further extended to covariates that are weakly dependent over time; the same studentization remains valid without an additional long-run variance estimator. Monte Carlo experiments evaluate the finite-sample size and power of the proposed test across different settings and demonstrate its favorable performance relative to the existing benchmark test. Applications to state tax competition and growth spillovers among OECD countries illustrate the practical relevance in testing for peer effects without specifying the interaction network.
item.dc:creator: Leheng Cai, Weijia Li, Xu Guo

item.title: Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Survey Weighting: Local Equivalent Weights in Structured Populations
item.description: arXiv:2610.20321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Regression-based survey weighting connects model-based population estimation with design-based inference through equivalent weights. For nonlinear models, equivalent weights can be defined locally through the sensitivity of a poststratified population estimator. However, conventional regression models may inadequately capture nonlinear relationships and complex interactions across sparse poststratification cells. We develop a survey-weighting framework based on hierarchical Gaussian process (HGP) regression, combining structured group-level effects with kernel-based smoothing to share information across related cells. We derive Gaussian posterior prediction formulas that exploit the structured covariance representation to reduce computational costs. We also establish a uniform convergence result for the posterior predictive mean under stated regularity conditions and construct local equivalent weights by matching the first-order sensitivity of a plug-in poststratified estimand to that of a weighted average of fitted response means, with both derivatives taken with respect to the latent mean-scale vector. Simulations show that HGP achieves lower population-weighted prediction error under nonparametric structure, whereas logistic regression performs well under correct parametric specification. Additional analyses examine sample size, frame coverage, subgroup prediction, and population-mean agreement. An application to the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study illustrates the method. Overall, this work extends local equivalent-weight construction to nonparametric modeling and provides a computational framework and conditional theoretical results for survey weighting in structured, sparse populations.
item.dc:creator: Seonghun Lee

item.title: Compound p-values for competition-based testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.20411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard competition-based multiple testing methods -- such as the knockoff filter and the target-decoy procedure -- are typically formulated as head-to-head competitions between a test unit and its assigned negative control unit. Motivated by real-world applications, which leverage any available negative controls, we study this competition-based framework in more intricate settings where competitions vary in size and structure. We propose new methods based on compound p-values -- p-values that are superuniform only on aggregate -- that enable powerful multiple testing with broader competition structures, via the Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg procedures. The former provides exact familywise error rate control, whereas the latter may incur a false discovery rate inflation factor, for which we derive upper bounds across a range of settings. We showcase the performance of our general competition-based testing methodology through extensive simulations and real-data applications, including analyses of virtual spatial transcriptomics and CRISPR screen datasets that exhibit precisely the complex competition structures that motivate our methods.
item.dc:creator: Junu Lee, Rina Foygel Barber, Richard J. Samworth, Zhimei Ren

item.title: Testing Conditional Distribution Equality Using Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.20447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conditional distribution equality testing is a core problem with applications in causal inference, model diagnostics, and transfer learning. Existing methods often lose power when the conditioning variable is high-dimensional. We propose a new test that leverages generative models to compare conditional distributions using both observed data and synthetic samples. A sample-splitting and studentization scheme is introduced to control estimation error. Under the null, the test statistic is asymptotically normal, and we establish local power against contiguous alternatives. Our theory under the null and fixed alternative requires only consistency of the learned conditional distribution, allowing for a broad class of generative models. Empirical results demonstrate accurate size control and strong power in high-dimensional settings compared to representative kernel-based conditional and joint two-sample tests.
item.dc:creator: Zekai Jin, Yi Zhang, Yun Yang, Xiaofeng Shao

item.title: Bayesian Causal Forests for Zero-Inflated Continuous Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2610.18889v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Estimating (heterogeneous) treatment effects is still challenging when the outcome is semicontinuous (i.e., exhibiting both a discrete point mass at zero and a skewed continuous distribution for positive values), despite the strong presence of this data type in real world settings. Existing methods either ignore the zero mass, impose fragile parametric assumptions, or suffer from extreme computational costs and data augmentation noise. This paper proposes Zero-Inflated Continuous Bayesian Causal Forests with Duan's Smearing (ZIC-BCF-Smear), a decoupled two-part nonparametric estimator that fits a Probit BCF on the full sample to model participation and a Gaussian BCF strictly on the active subpopulation to model positive intensity. Subpopulation Propensity Adjustment (SPA) mitigates regularization-induced confounding within the active subpopulation, and Duan's non-parametric smearing estimator re-transforms predictions to the response scale, bypassing the fragile scale multipliers of parametric models. A comprehensive simulation benchmark shows that ZIC-BCF-Smear matches well-specified parametric models without their assumptions and remains stable and calibrated where competitors either diverge or pathologically over-cover for nonlinear data. The method is then applied to individual-participant data from the SPECTRUM randomized phase III head-and-neck cancer trial, estimating the causal effect of assignment to panitumumab plus chemotherapy on the number of days patients spend with severe toxicity, an outcome for which a quarter of patients contribute an exact zero. Panitumumab assignment raises that burden by about ten days per patient under the trial's own differential treatment duration, and the decoupled structure localizes the effect mainly in the positive-intensity part rather than in whether the reconstructed severe-AE burden is positive.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Gobato Souto, Eric Wang, Igor Shuryak

item.title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology
item.description: arXiv:2610.19074v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network-width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (TNN) prior with width-dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural-network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean-square error (MSE) $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ at expected computational cost $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger-scale applications, we further introduce S-MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission-code-anon/mlpmmh-anon.
item.dc:creator: Neil K. Chada, Simon Cotter, Kody J. H. Law, Xinzhu Liang

item.title: Neural Supervised Clustering for Learning Individualized Treatment Rules with Many Treatments
item.description: arXiv:2610.19104v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learning an individualized treatment rule (ITR) with many treatments requires estimating treatment-specific effects from limited observations per arm. Treatments with similar conditional responses can share information, but linear contrast models may miss nonlinear heterogeneity. We propose nonlinear supervised clustering fusion (NSCF), a neural Q-learning framework with a shared nonlinear covariate representation and low-dimensional treatment embeddings. Pairwise fusion groups treatments with similar learned contrasts, yielding an ITR and an interpretable partition. An alternating algorithm combines neural training, embedding fusion, validation-based partition selection, and unpenalized grouped refitting. NSCF lowers regret relative to a strong neural reference in nonlinear exact-sharing simulations; perturbations characterize the limits of hard sharing. In a melanoma xenograft application, NSCF improves average policy value over the neural reference. These results support nonlinear representation learning with supervised treatment fusion when treatment effects exhibit shared structure.
item.dc:creator: Daixi Huang, Yixin Yuan, Yifan Dai, Yufeng Liu

item.title: Student Copula Markov Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.19135v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper extends the applicability of probabilistic graphical models to non Gaussian data. It establishes a characterization of the pairwise Markov property in undirected probabilistic graphical models in terms of copula densities. Building on this characterization, we derive a necessary condition for the pairwise Markov property in Student copula Markov networks. An Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm (ECM) is provided to facilitate the penalized maximum likelihood estimation and graph selection. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated through simulation studies, which demonstrate its effectiveness in estimating model parameters and recovering the underlying graph structure.
item.dc:creator: Salha Mamane, Cheikh Tidiane Seck

item.title: Generalizing Identifiability Results in Causal Discovery from Complete Data to Missing Data Settings
item.description: arXiv:2610.19211v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While causal discovery methods have matured for complete data, such algorithms for handling missing values remain limited. We establish general sufficient conditions under which causal graphs remain identifiable (i.e., uniquely determined from the available data distribution) under various missingness categories, including Missing Not At Random, and provide a framework to extend correctness guarantees from causal discovery algorithms for complete data to missing data settings. Our results show that identifiability of causal graphs with no unobserved confounders is preserved when (1) missingness mechanisms do not causally interact, (2) no variable directly causes its own missingness, and (3) either faithfulness holds for missingness mechanisms, or they follow generalized linear models. Guided by these theoretical results, we introduce two asymptotically correct algorithms for Additive Noise Models (ANMs) that recover the underlying causal graph and provide consistent parameter estimates.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Ceriscioli, Shohei Shimizu, Mallika Gupta, Karthika Mohan

item.title: Multi-Sensitive Distributional Fairness: Joint Wasserstein Audits and Shapley Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2610.19252v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fairness audits with several sensitive attributes are often performed one coordinate at a time. This can miss purely intersectional disparities: a score may be independent of each sensitive coordinate while depending on their joint profile. We study distributional demographic parity for a real-valued score using one-dimensional Wasserstein geometry. We distinguish two complementary constructions. Conditional and sequential audits characterize joint parity through their zero sets, but their positive values do not generally decompose a fixed joint Wasserstein disparity. By contrast, full-cell conditional quantile functions define a Hilbert-valued random variable whose variance is the joint disparity. Conditional expectations of this quantile process induce a monotone information game: every reveal order yields an exact martingale decomposition of the same joint disparity, while Shapley values provide an order-free attribution across sensitive attributes. Under independent sensitive attributes, the game reduces to a Hoeffding-ANOVA decomposition and Shapley splits each interaction energy equally among its members; under dependence, orthogonality is lost and explicit formulas reveal suppression and redundancy effects that marginal audits can hide. We give fixed-grid estimators and permutation calibration, and illustrate the framework on synthetic examples and ACSIncome. The resulting framework separates three questions that are often conflated: whether joint distributional parity holds, how a fixed joint disparity decomposes along an information path, and how that disparity can be attributed across sensitive coordinates without privileging an ordering.
item.dc:creator: Agathe Fernandes Machado, Charlotte Jamotton, Arthur Charpentier

item.title: On Local Inference for Functionals of Ill-Posed Inverse Problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.19350v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study inference for continuous linear functionals of solutions to ill-posed inverse problems, including Euclidean parameters arising in nonparametric instrumental variables, proximal causal inference, and shadow-variable models. Although pointwise root-$n$ inference is possible under standard conditions, we show that this need not translate into locally reliable inference. Under a model imposing only minimal regularity conditions, the target is Hellinger discontinuous when both inverse problems are ill-posed: arbitrarily small changes in the data-generating law can produce arbitrarily large changes in the target, ruling out informative locally uniform inference. Imposing a uniform bound on a minimum-norm solution restores Hellinger continuity under regularity conditions, but does not by itself ensure stable root-n inference. If, in addition, both inverse problems are ill-posed and the solution whose norm is uniformly bounded is nonunique at a law $P_0$, then under regularity conditions the target fails to be pathwise differentiable; consequently, asymptotically linear estimators exhibit nonvanishing root-$n$ bias under some local alternatives, causing Wald confidence intervals to undercover asymptotically. Under regularity conditions, pathwise differentiability is restored if the uniformly bounded solution is unique at $P_0$. It is also restored, regardless of uniqueness, under the stronger requirement that the corresponding solution satisfy a uniformly bounded $\beta$-source condition for some $\beta$>0. We relate these regimes to very weak, weak, and strong identification in instrumental variables models.
item.dc:creator: Ellen Graham, Andrea Rotnitzky

item.title: SULA: Robust Langevin Sampling via Drift-Diffusion Saturation
item.description: arXiv:2610.19670v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) and its stochastic-gradient variant, SGLD, are workhorses of modern Bayesian machine learning, but can be fragile when faced with a target distribution possessing a non-Lipschitz drift. In such settings, the expected squared jump distance can grow rapidly, leading to numerical instability or the need for prohibitively small step-sizes. We propose the saturated unadjusted Langevin algorithm (SULA) that pairs a saturated gradient drift with a gradient-informed state-dependent diffusion, while preserving first-order consistency with the Langevin diffusion. The drift and diffusion terms are chosen to guarantee that the one-step squared update is independent of the gradient. Consequently, SULA is robust to the choice of step-size and preserves estimation and prediction quality. We provide sufficient conditions under which SULA with a step-size $h$ converges weakly to the Langevin diffusion at the standard $O(h)$ rate, the SULA chain is geometrically ergodic, and that the bias of its invariant measure relative to the target is $O(h)$. Further, we develop SG-SULA, a stochastic-gradient version of SULA that rescales the stochastic gradient using a Gaussian CDF correction under Gaussianity of the gradient noise. Numerical experiments on various examples demonstrate SULA's robustness to tuning and SG-SULA's improved predictive performance.
item.dc:creator: Ritik Soni, Dootika Vats

item.title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters
item.description: arXiv:2610.19888v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.
item.dc:creator: Daniel S. Han, Vaishnavi Ananthanarayanan, Matthew J. Simpson

item.title: Principal stratification with continuous treatments and continuous post-treatment variables
item.description: arXiv:2309.14486v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Principal stratification (PS) is a commonly used approach for understanding the mechanisms through which a treatment affects an outcome. The goal of this work is to extend the PS framework to studies with continuous treatments, which introduces a number of both challenges and opportunities in terms of defining causal effects and performing inference. This manuscript provides multiple key methodological contributions: 1) we introduce principal causal estimands for continuous treatments that provide insights into different causal mechanisms, 2) we show that nonparametric identification is possible under a principal ignorability assumption, but only under a restrictive assumption on the joint distribution of potential mediators, which can be dropped under certain parametric assumptions, 3) we utilize nonparametric Bayesian models for the joint distribution of the potential mediating variables to mitigate issues from model misspecification, and 4) we provide theoretical justification for utilizing an outcome model to identify the joint distribution of the potential mediating variables, and show that this is only possible if a principal ignorability assumption is violated. Lastly, we illustrate our methodology by applying it to a novel study of the relationship between the economy and arrest rates, and how this is potentially mediated by police capacity.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Antonelli, Minxuan Wu, Fabrizia Mealli, Brenden Beck, Alessandra Mattei

item.title: Controlling the false discovery rate in high-dimensional linear models using model-X knockoffs and $p$-values
item.description: arXiv:2505.16124v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a novel multiple testing methodology for controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) in high-dimensional linear models that integrates model-X knockoff techniques with debiased penalized regression estimators. At the foundation of our methodology, we construct and study two sets of naturally paired high-dimensional test statistics and the associated $p$-values for evaluating the same null hypotheses. The first set is shown to be asymptotically mutually independent, justifying the use of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. We further exploit the pairing structure through a two-step procedure aimed at improving power. Our theoretical results establish the key properties of the framework with respect to asymptotic FDR control and formally characterize the associated power gains of the two-step procedure. Importantly, our framework accommodates general dependence in the design matrix. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our methods outperform existing approaches -- particularly those relying on empirical FDP estimates -- in both power and FDR control accuracy, with notable gains in settings involving weaker signals, small sample sizes, or low target FDR levels.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Chang, Chenlong Li, Cheng Yong Tang, Zhengtian Zhu

item.title: Measuring frailty in the elderly: an indicator based on a super-classifier
item.description: arXiv:2506.22349v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Identifying frail older adults in an ageing population is essential for improving healthcare services. This study proposes a composite indicator to assess individual frailty levels using administrative healthcare data. Given the complex and multidimensional nature of frailty, a multi-outcome approach is adopted. Following an extensive literature review, a set of adverse health events is selected as proxies for frailty. These events were modelled using logistic classifiers, with frailty determinants (associated to adverse health events, selected using a gradient tree boosting) serving as covariates. The sensitivity and specificity of each classifier is used to compose their combined likelihood. From this, we derive an indicator capable of quantifying frailty across the population. The indicator shows robust performance across multiple outcomes and over time. Its primary innovation lies in allowing the use of diverse and outcome-specific sets of frailty determinants without any structural constraint. Overall, we offer an effective tool for quantifying frailty among older adults, potentially supporting health authorities in the prevention of frailty-related adverse events.
item.dc:creator: Sara Rebottini, Margherita Silan, Pietro Belloni

item.title: Density Discontinuity Regression
item.description: arXiv:2507.05581v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many policies hinge on a continuous variable exceeding a threshold, prompting strategic behavior by agents to stay on the favorable side. This creates density discontinuities at cutoffs, evident in contexts like taxable income, corporate regulations, and academic grading. Existing methods detect these discontinuities, but systematic approaches to examine how they vary with observable characteristics are lacking. We propose a novel, interpretable Bayesian framework that jointly estimates both the log-density ratio at the cutoff and the local shape of the density, as functions of covariates, within a data-driven window. This formulation yields regression-style estimates of covariate effects on the discontinuity. An adaptive window selection balances bias and variance. Our approach improves upon common methods that target only the log-density ratio around the threshold while ignoring the local density shape. We constrain the density jump to be non-negative, reflecting that agents would not aim to be on the losing side of the threshold. Applied to corporate shareholder voting data, our method identifies substantial variation in strategic behavior, notably stronger discontinuities for proposals facing negative recommendations from Institutional Shareholder Services, larger firms, and firms with lower analyst coverage. Overall, our method provides an interpretable framework to quantify heterogeneous agent responses to threshold-based policies.
item.dc:creator: Surya T Tokdar, Rik Sen, Haoliang Zheng, Shuangjie Zhang

item.title: Relative Bias Under Imperfect Identification in Observational Causal Inference
item.description: arXiv:2507.23743v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To conduct causal inference in observational settings, researchers must rely on certain identifying assumptions. In practice, these assumptions are unlikely to hold exactly. This paper considers the bias of selection-on-observables, instrumental variables, and proximal inference estimates under violations of their identifying assumptions. We develop bias expressions for IV and proximal inference that show how violations of their respective assumptions are amplified by any unmeasured confounding in the outcome variable. We propose a set of sensitivity tools that quantify the sensitivity of different identification strategies, and an augmented bias contour plot visualizes the relationship between these strategies. We argue that the act of choosing an identification strategy implicitly expresses a belief about the degree of violations that must be present in alternative identification strategies. Even when researchers intend to conduct an IV or proximal analysis, a sensitivity analysis comparing different identification strategies can help to better understand the implications of each set of assumptions. Throughout, we compare the different approaches on a re-analysis of the impact of state surveillance on the incidence of protest in Communist Poland.
item.dc:creator: Melody Huang, Cory McCartan

item.title: Bootstrap inference in factor-augmented regressions with weak factors
item.description: arXiv:2510.00947v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we develop bootstrap methods for factor-augmented regressions with potentially weak common components, allowing signal eigenvalues to diverge at heterogeneous rates $N^{\alpha_k}$, where $0<\alpha_k\leq1$, $k=1,\ldots,r$. The regression estimator targets a rotation of the latent parameter vector that may be data dependent, while factor estimation can induce asymptotic bias. The proposed procedure directly constructs the rotation-specific target in the bootstrap world, avoiding the additional randomness induced by existing bootstrap methods. Bootstrap distributional validity is established for two data-dependent targets and a signal-dependent population target, where studentization provides asymptotically pivotal statistics for both analytical and bootstrap bias-corrected estimators. The analysis also distinguishes distributional approximation relative to a data-dependent target from inference on fixed population restrictions and introduces a bootstrap diagnostic for rotation uncertainty (RU) when signal eigenvalues are close. Monte Carlo experiments show improved bias correction, gains from bootstrap distributional approximation, and demonstrate that inference distortions from small signal eigengaps dissipate quickly with $T$ for fixed targets, in contrast to the persistent distortions under random rotations. An application to excess bond return predictability illustrates the practical importance of bootstrap distributional approximation and rotation uncertainty for inference on individual factor coefficients.
item.dc:creator: Peiyun Jiang, Takashi Yamagata

item.title: Living Synthetic Benchmarks: A Neutral and Cumulative Framework for Simulation Studies
item.description: arXiv:2510.19489v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulation studies are widely used to evaluate statistical methods. However, new methods are often introduced and evaluated using data-generating mechanisms (DGMs) devised by the same authors. This coupling creates misaligned incentives, e.g., the need to demonstrate the superiority of new methods, potentially compromising the neutrality of simulation studies. Furthermore, results of simulation studies are often difficult to compare due to differences in DGMs, competing methods, and performance measures. This fragmentation can lead to conflicting conclusions, hinder methodological progress, and delay the adoption of effective methods. To address these challenges, we introduce the concept of living synthetic benchmarks. The key idea is to disentangle method and simulation study development and continuously update the benchmark whenever a new DGM, method, or performance measure becomes available. This separation benefits the neutrality of method evaluation, emphasizes the development of both methods and DGMs, and enables systematic comparisons. In this paper, we outline a blueprint for building and maintaining such benchmarks, discuss the technical and organizational challenges of implementation, and demonstrate feasibility with a prototype benchmark for publication bias adjustment methods. We conclude that living synthetic benchmarks have the potential to foster neutral, reproducible, and cumulative evaluation of methods, benefiting both method developers and users.
item.dc:creator: Franti\v{s}ek Barto\v{s}, Samuel Pawel, Bj\"orn S. Siepe

item.title: Approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic hybrid systems with empirically observed ergodic behaviour
item.description: arXiv:2511.11782v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Piecewise diffusion Markov processes (PDifMPs) form a versatile class of stochastic hybrid systems that combine continuous diffusion processes with discrete event-driven dynamics, enabling flexible modelling of complex real-world hybrid phenomena. The practical utility of PDifMP models, however, depends critically on accurate estimation of their underlying parameters. In this work, we present a novel framework for parameter inference in PDifMPs based on approximate Bayesian computation (ABC). Our contributions are threefold. First, we provide detailed simulation algorithms for PDifMP sample paths. Second, we extend existing ABC summary statistics for diffusion processes to account for the hybrid nature of PDifMPs, showing particular effectiveness for ergodic systems. Third, we demonstrate our approach on several representative example PDifMPs that empirically exhibit ergodic behaviour. Our results show that the proposed ABC method reliably recovers model parameters across all examples, even in challenging scenarios where only partial information on jumps and diffusion is available or when parameters appear in state-dependent jump rate functions. These findings highlight the potential of ABC as a practical tool for inference in various complex stochastic hybrid systems.
item.dc:creator: Sascha Desmettre, Agnes Mallinger, Amira Meddah, Irene Tubikanec

item.title: Shortest fixed-width confidence intervals for a bounded parameter: The Push algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2511.13694v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a method for computing optimal fixed-width confidence intervals for a single, bounded parameter, extending a method for the binomial due to Asparaouhov and Lorden, who called it the Push algorithm. The method produces the shortest possible non-decreasing confidence interval for a given confidence level, and if the Push interval does not exist for a given width and level, then no such interval exists. The method applies to any bounded parameter that is discrete, or is continuous for which interval probabilities are quasiconcave. We demonstrate the method on the binomial, hypergeometric, and normal distributions with our available R package. In each of these distributions the proposed method outperforms the standard ones, and in the latter case even improves upon the $z$-interval. We apply the proposed method to World Health Organization (WHO) data on tobacco use.
item.dc:creator: Jay Bartroff, Asmit Chakraborty

item.title: Associating High-Dimensional Longitudinal Datasets through an Efficient Cross-Covariance Decomposition
item.description: arXiv:2601.13405v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding associations between paired high-dimensional longitudinal datasets is a fundamental yet challenging problem arising across scientific domains, including longitudinal multi-omic studies. The difficulty stems from the complex, time-varying cross-covariance structure coupled with high dimensionality, which complicates both model formulation and statistical estimation for association discovery. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework called Functional-Aggregated Cross-covariance Decomposition (FACD), tailored to analyzing associations in paired high-dimensional longitudinal datasets through a statistically efficient procedure. Unlike existing methods that are limited to low-dimensional data or rely on parametric modeling of temporal dynamics, FACD is capable of learning temporal structure by aggregating high-dimensional signals and accommodating variable selection to identify the most temporally associated features across datasets. We establish statistical guarantees for FACD and demonstrate its advantages over existing approaches through extensive simulation studies. Finally, we apply FACD to a longitudinal multi-omic human study, revealing blood molecules with time-varying associations across omic layers during acute exercise.
item.dc:creator: Jianbin Tan, Pixu Shi

item.title: Testing Cumulative Treatment Effects in Continuous Time with ODE Dynamics and Noisy Observations
item.description: arXiv:2602.02246v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a semiparametric continuous time inferential framework for testing cumulative treatment effects, including both immediate and carryover effects. The latent state process is modeled by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) whose drift depends on state and treatment, while the observed data are noisy measurements of this latent state at irregular, multi resolution time points. We define the average treatment effect (ATE) as the difference of expected cumulative outcomes under the always treat and always control policies and establish its identifiability from observational data. More generally, the framework accommodates contrasts between arbitrary deterministic stationary treatment policies, including clinically motivated threshold policies, with the always treat versus never treat comparison as the leading special case. A two step estimation procedure first recovers the latent state trajectories and their derivatives via spline smoothing, then solves a continuous time estimating equation derived from the infinitesimal generator of the ODE. We prove asymptotic normality of the resulting test statistic under explicit rate conditions on the spline estimator. The resulting test admits asymptotically valid inference under noisy, irregularly sampled observations, providing a studentized statistic with a standard $N(0,1)$ limit. Simulations show that the proposed method demonstrates improved stability and power over discrete time alternatives in noisy and multi resolution settings, with comparable performance under clean regular grids. We apply the method to the OhioT1DM diabetes dataset to evaluate cumulative effects of insulin treatments on glucose levels.
item.dc:creator: Jiuchen Zhang, Annie Qu

item.title: Robustifying Empirical Bayes
item.description: arXiv:2603.00704v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two strategies are explored for robustifying classical denoising procedures for the Gaussian sequence model. First, the Hodges and Lehmann (1952) restricted Bayes approach is used to reduce sensitivity to the specification of the initial prior distribution. Second, alternatives to the Gaussian noise assumption are explored. In both cases proposals of Huber (1964) and Mallows (1978) play a crucial role.
item.dc:creator: Roger Koenker, Jiaying Gu

item.title: Sign-Flipping Score Tests for Fixed Effects in Multivariate Clustered Data
item.description: arXiv:2604.27907v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Standard parametric inference on fixed effects in multivariate linear mixed models can be sensitive to covariance misspecification, particularly with multivariate responses. We propose clip, a clusterwise conditional resampling procedure based on effective scores and transformation-specific standardization. The procedure may use a working covariance to improve efficiency, but its validity does not require correct specification. When covariance parameters are estimated, they are estimated only once and held fixed across transformations. Together with synchronous transformations that avoid modeling between-response covariance, this facilitates joint inference for high-dimensional multivariate responses. Under a correctly specified marginal mean and suitable regularity conditions, we establish asymptotic validity for independent, heterogeneous clusters and derive a quantitative bound relating approximation accuracy to the magnitude and heterogeneity of clusterwise score contributions. Simulations show reliable type I error control and competitive power. An electroencephalography application illustrates simultaneous inference across correlated outcomes.
item.dc:creator: Angela Andreella, Livio Finos

item.title: Change-point detection in variance-covariance matrix
item.description: arXiv:2605.12881v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the joint estimation of change-point locations and the sparsity pattern of the variance-covariance matrix, which is assumed to evolve in a piecewise constant manner. By applying Group Fused LASSO and LASSO penalties to the squared Frobenius norm, we estimate both the covariance structure and the change points. Adaptive weights are incorporated into the penalty terms to enhance change-point detection and covariance estimation accuracy. We establish the conditions under which the estimated change points and the sparse estimators within each segment are consistent. To solve the resulting optimization problem efficiently, we develop an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) whose updates reduce to computationally tractable subproblems. The performance of the proposed method is illustrated through synthetic and real-data experiments, including comparisons with several competing procedures.
item.dc:creator: Ying Lin, Benjamin Poignard

item.title: Robust inference for risk heterogeneity under group imbalance
item.description: arXiv:2606.00797v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Population-level heterogeneity is ubiquitous in biomedical data, where differences across demographic or clinical subgroups can substantially alter risk patterns. For example, in intensive care unit (ICU) studies, the mortality risk associated with specific admission diagnoses can vary across ethnic groups. Existing approaches for detecting risk heterogeneity are often sensitive to baseline model misspecification and regularization bias, both of which commonly arise in practice. In this paper, we propose a robust framework for inferring risk heterogeneity between two populations using Neyman orthogonality, which yields estimators that are locally insensitive to nuisance parameter estimation error. The proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and simulation studies demonstrate that in finite samples our method substantially reduces bias and improves inferential stability compared with standard likelihood-based approaches. In an application to the eICU Collaborative Research Database, our method reveals clinically meaningful ethnicity-specific heterogeneity in admission diagnoses for in-hospital mortality that standard likelihood-based methods fail to detect.
item.dc:creator: Mengqi Xu, Subha Maity, Joel Dubin

item.title: Improving Mendelian Randomization Analysis by Instrument Borrowing from Auxiliary Outcome Traits
item.description: arXiv:2607.16086v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mendelian randomization (MR) infers causal effects of exposures on outcomes using genetic variants as instrumental variables, but existing methods remain vulnerable to bias and loss of power when instruments are invalid. We hypothesize that closely related outcome traits share a large overlap in their valid instruments for a given exposure, so that borrowing instruments across such traits can yield more robust MR inference. To operationalize this, we introduce a novel coheterogeneity statistic, together with its asymptotic theory under different paradigms that allows for a growing number of instruments as the sample size increases, to identify secondary outcome traits likely to share valid instruments with the primary trait. We then propose extensions of two popular methods, MR-Mode and MR-PRESSO, that improve inference for the primary trait by exploiting a secondary trait. Extensive simulations show that the coheterogeneity statistic has the expected finite-sample properties and that instrument-borrowing methods consistently outperform their standard counterparts, with gains increasing as the overlap in valid instruments grows. Applications to established positive and negative control hypotheses indicate improved control of type I error and increased power. We further illustrate practical utility by revisiting the long-debated hypothesis of the causal effect of vitamin D on cardiometabolic traits.
item.dc:creator: Anagh Chattopadhyay, Nilanjan Chatterjee

item.title: Log-regularly varying scale mixture of asymmetric Laplaces for robust Bayesian quantile regression
item.description: arXiv:2608.25186v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian quantile regression based on the asymmetric Laplace (AL) distribution can be sensitive to extreme observations because of its exponentially decaying tails. We propose a robust error distribution constructed as a finite mixture of the AL distribution and a log-Pareto scale mixture of asymmetric Laplace distributions (LPAL). Unlike a direct log-Pareto extension of the normal location-scale representation of the AL distribution, the proposed AL-LPAL mixture preserves the prescribed quantile and exhibits log-regularly varying behavior in both tails. The LPAL component also has an unbounded density at the target quantile, yielding a distribution that combines sharp central concentration with super-heavy tails. We establish posterior robustness under arbitrarily extreme contamination and provide sufficient conditions for the existence of posterior moments of the regression coefficients and scale parameter. For posterior computation, we develop a Gibbs sampler using latent-variable augmentations and a computationally efficient mean-field variational Bayes approximation. Simulation studies show that the proposed method is competitive under moderate contamination and maintains stable point estimation with comparatively concentrated posterior intervals, particularly when severe contamination affects the quantile of interest. Applications to carbon dioxide and Boston housing data, using the same preprocessing as existing robust Bayesian quantile regression analyses, show favorable predictive performance across nearly all quantile levels and loss criteria considered.
item.dc:creator: Dongu Han, Genya Kobayashi, Shonosuke Sugasawa

item.title: Non-Invariance in Nested Prediction Models under Selective Predictor Availability
item.description: arXiv:2609.02836v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We used nested models as a framework for characterising the consequences of a selectively measured predictor in clinical prediction models. In this framework, a model containing predictors available in the target population is referred to as the restricted model, while the extended model additionally includes a selectively measured predictor. We show that non-invariance in the restricted model between selected patients and the target population decomposes into components due to omission of the additional predictor, potential residual non-invariance, and their interaction. This framework is extended to a predictor measured via multiple routes of selection resulting in collider structures. We further show that imputation based on the conditional distribution of the additional predictor in the selected population transfers the restricted-model non-invariance to the imputed extended model as imputation bias. In a forthcoming version, this framework will be illustrated using real world and simulated data. The framework provides a formal basis for understanding how selective predictor measurement affects generalisability of clinical prediction models using routinely collected health data.
item.dc:creator: Marc Delord

item.title: Estimating Causal Treatment Effects in Placebo-Controlled Randomized Clinical Trials When High Placebo Response is Anticipated
item.description: arXiv:2609.09377v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials (RCTs), the placebo response significantly modifies treatment effects and diminishes the intention-to-treat (ITT) treatment effect, $\Delta_{ITT}$. This study presents a novel two-stage framework for estimating the standardized causal treatment effect, $\Delta_{STD}$, among the ITT population, under the assumption that their placebo responses are similar to the levels of self-administering medication at home. The first stage employs a real-world, pragmatic, single-blinded placebo lead-in to measure placebo responses to levels expected during routine at-home use. This is achieved by preserving the participants' expectations and controlling for trial-related factors that inflate the responses. In the second stage, a double-blinded randomized phase is used to estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) as a function of placebo response levels and other important effect modifiers. To facilitate CATE estimation, the prognostic scores, defined as the expected placebo responses, are used for dimension reduction. The causal estimand $\Delta_{STD}$ is computed by integrating the CATE function over the distribution of the expected placebo response levels from stage one and other modifiers. We further derive theoretical values for $\Delta_{ITT}-\Delta_{STD}$ to quantify the underestimated treatment benefit due to high placebo responses. The validity and statistical performance of the proposed framework are evaluated through comprehensive simulations.
item.dc:creator: Yang Song, Yunzhe Qian, Chanmin Kim, Gheorghe Doros

item.title: The Critical Line Algorithm and the Constrained LASSO: One Curve, Two Literatures
item.description: arXiv:2609.25704v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many statistical procedures compute an entire solution path rather than a single estimator. For one class the path is piecewise linear, traced corner to corner by an active-set homotopy. Two of its members coincide exactly: under $\Sigma=X^\top X$ and $\mu=X^\top y$ the gross-exposure-constrained mean--variance program and the constrained LASSO trace the same piecewise-linear curve, and they keep doing so under arbitrary linear equality and inequality constraints. Which parameter is swept, a leverage budget or a return tilt, is not a choice the curve notices: under a homogeneous mandate the two sweeps differ by a scalar. A mandate that holds the portfolio invested costs a radial rescaling instead, and the efficient frontier is that curve rescaled; its corners pass unnoticed because the frontier is continuously differentiable where they fall. We give the map between the two parametrisations and the single way it degenerates. That mean--variance selection and the LASSO instantiate one parametric quadratic program is prior art (G\"artner, Jaggi and Maria, 2012). The Critical Line Algorithm itself lies off that route, and the correspondence established here is new. The identity is one of curves, not of statistical experiments. The map between the parametrisations is computed from the data, so the geometry of the path transfers while quantities averaged over the response do not. We cross that boundary deliberately and give the degrees of freedom of the constrained fit under arbitrary linear constraints. In the long-only, fully invested case it is the expected number of holdings away from a bound, less one.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Schmelzer, Trevor Hastie

item.title: Amortized ratio-estimation importance sampling and localized simulation-based calibration for intractable likelihoods
item.description: arXiv:2609.39712v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider simulation-based Bayesian inference (SBI) for the parameters of models with intractable likelihoods but tractable forward simulation. Building on Gaussian mixtures-of-experts surrogates, as a first contribution we develop a sequential procedure to estimate the posterior, incorporating an importance sampling step that introduces a locally amortized likelihood-to-evidence ratio estimator. The local amortization allows the ratio estimator to be evaluated at new parameter--data pairs from a local (data-dependent) design, without re-estimation, which is particularly convenient for our second contribution. The second contribution is localized simulation-based calibration (SBC). Localized SBC provides a graphical diagnostic of calibration over neighborhoods that are deliberately broader than the available posterior, at low additional computational cost. Rather than repeatedly running the full inference procedure for each simulated pseudo-observation, localized SBC fits the local surrogate and ratio estimator only once for each local design, and reuses them across all pseudo-observations. This approach is particularly appealing for SBI applications. We evaluate both contributions on three case studies, including a real-data epidemiological application.
item.dc:creator: Umberto Picchini

item.title: When Treatments Spill Over: A Neural Framework for Spatiotemporal Causal Effect Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.16086v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real-world public health policies are often enacted by local jurisdictions, but their effects can ripple through connected populations. For causal evaluation, this creates a difficult spatiotemporal problem: intermittent policy updates create path-level treatments, and because spillover depends on neighboring treatment paths along with the focal-unit's own history, controlling time-varying confounding requires high-dimensional, multimodal information from both sources. To address this challenge, we develop a neural spatiotemporal spillover framework that extends potential-outcome causal analysis to networked policy-systems with unit-level effects and structured interference. The framework indexes each unit's potential outcomes through own-treatment and neighborhood spillover-exposure paths, yielding direct, spillover, and total effects. We introduce an LSTM-based representation-learning encoder that integrates each unit's own and neighborhood histories into compact sequential summaries for downstream modeling and causal estimation. These summaries feed a self-normalized kernel inverse-probability-weighting estimator for continuous spillover exposure. Beyond theoretical guarantees, simulations show improved performance over outcome-regression baselines; in a practically motivated county-level COVID-19 policy study, the framework finds both business-and-economic restrictions and education-and-childcare policies associated with lower subsequent case burden, with larger estimates for business-and-economic restrictions. Overall, it provides a scalable, policy-interpretable framework for evaluating unit-level effects in high-dimensional, multimodal spatiotemporal systems when interventions spill over across space and time.
item.dc:creator: Shaohui Zhang, Jiasheng Shi, Jing Huang

item.title: Multivariate L\'evy Adaptive B-Spline Regression
item.description: arXiv:2108.11863v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose Multivariate L\'evy Adaptive B-Spline Regression (MLABS), a Bayesian nonparametric regression model designed to capture nonlinear effects, interactions, and locally varying features of multivariate functions. MLABS represents the regression function as a random sum of low-order tensor-product B-spline basis functions under a finite L\'evy random measure prior. The resulting representation adapts to the complexity and local structure of the regression function while favoring a sparse basis representation. For posterior inference, we develop a reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm with Bayesian backfitting, collapsed trans-dimensional updates, and residual-guided proposals. These computational strategies are designed to improve posterior exploration across basis configurations of varying dimensions and structures. We also establish approximation bounds for functions with low-order interactions and heterogeneous smoothness. These bounds relate approximation accuracy to the number of basis terms. Simulation studies show that MLABS achieves competitive predictive performance across a wide range of regression settings, including high-dimensional problems. MLABS also demonstrates robust predictive performance across benchmark real datasets. In an environmental-mixture application, it attains predictive accuracy comparable to Bayesian kernel machine regression at substantially lower computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Sewon Park, Jaeyong Lee, Jeunghun Oh

item.title: Inverse Probability Weighting-based Mediation Analysis for Microbiome Data
item.description: arXiv:2110.02440v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Motivation: Mediation analysis is an important tool for elucidating causal mechanisms in biomedical research and has recently gained increasing attention in microbiome studies. Motivated by a microbiome study of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients, we investigate whether the effect of induction chemotherapy intensity on infection status is mediated through gut microbial taxa. This problem poses substantial methodological challenges due to the high dimensionality, zero inflation, and dependence of microbial mediators, as well as the presence of an exposure-induced mediator--outcome confounder, antibiotic use. Results: To address these challenges, we propose a novel nonparametric identification formula for the interventional indirect effect, a causal mediation estimand that remains identifiable in the presence of exposure-induced mediator--outcome confounding. Building on this identification result, we develop an inverse probability weighting estimator and construct standard normal bootstrap confidence intervals for inference. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate effect estimation and maintains appropriate type I error rates and power in finite samples. Application to the AML microbiome study provides evidence of a statistically significant interventional indirect effect of induction chemotherapy intensity on infection risk through alterations in the gut microbiome. Availability and implementation: The R code for the simulation studies is available at https://github.com/YX-ZHANG-1/CausalMediationMicrobiome and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21960802.
item.dc:creator: Yuexia Zhang, Jian Wang, Jiayi Shen, Jessica Galloway-Pena, Samuel Shelburne, Linbo Wang, Jianhua Hu

item.title: Stereographic Multiple-Try Metropolis
item.description: arXiv:2505.12487v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multiple-proposal MCMC algorithms have recently gained attention for their potential to improve performance, especially through parallel implementation on modern hardware. We introduce Stereographic Multiple-Try Metropolis (SMTM), a novel family of gradient-free algorithms designed for sampling high-dimensional distributions. By integrating multiple-try Metropolis (MTM) with the stereographic MCMC framework, SMTM overcomes the traditional limitations of MTM, particularly its pathological convergence behavior often observed in high dimensions. For both light-tailed and heavy-tailed targets, SMTM not only outperforms classical MTM and the existing stereographic random-walk Metropolis but also demonstrates strong robustness to tuning. These advantages are supported by high-dimensional scaling analysis and validated through extensive simulation studies.
item.dc:creator: Zhihao Wang, Jun Yang

item.title: Beyond Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Accelerators: Directed Evidence for Adaptive Sustainability Portfolios
item.description: arXiv:2601.20875v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Governments and development partners often seek Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) "accelerators" whose progress can propagate gains across human well-being, institutions, resources, and environmental priorities. Such claims require evidence on direction, timing, robustness, and trade-offs, not only network connectivity. We map directed SDG interdependence using a balanced panel of 114 countries observed annually from 2000 to 2024. Because the goal series are persistent, trending, and cross-sectionally dependent, we combine Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger non-causality tests on first-differenced series with false-discovery control across 272 directed goal pairs, and panel local projections with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors for 31 theory-derived indicator linkages. We find 84 directed linkages after correction: 40 synergies and 44 trade-offs. This dense structure does not support a universal accelerator. Driver-receiver rankings are fragile across lag orders, centrality metrics, bootstrap resampling, and alternative dependence controls; only peace and strong institutions as a net receiver and poverty reduction as an effect-size-weighted driver are distinguishable in the bootstrap screen. Two local-projection pathways are supported, both leading to lower child mortality, and the education-child-health association is corroborated in independent World Development Indicators data across 183 countries. The policy implication is not to abandon SDG integration, but to replace fixed global accelerator rankings with adaptive portfolios built around supported, time-lagged linkages and monitored constituent indicators.
item.dc:creator: Md Muhtasim Munif Fahim, Md Jahid Hasan Imran, Md. Naim Molla, Luknath Debnath, Tonmoy Shil, Ehsanul Bashar Pranto, Md Mostafizur Rahman Likhon, Md Shafin Sanyan Saad, Md. Rezaul Karim

item.title: Two Gaussians, Too Many: A bootstrap-based approach to assess identifiability in non-Gaussian structural vector autoregressions
item.description: arXiv:2607.17275v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Normality pre-tests on reduced-form innovations cannot detect whether two or more underlying structural shocks are Gaussian, and hence cannot detect a failure of identification in non-Gaussian SVARs. We propose a bootstrap-based approach that reveals such a failure. Under the null of valid identification and certain regularity conditions, the conditional bootstrap distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator of the impact matrix is asymptotically normal, so the diagnostic reduces to a normality test on the bootstrap replications. The impact-matrix estimator remains consistent and asymptotically normal when one shock is Gaussian and its shape parameter lies on the boundary of the parameter space, so the diagnostic is valid across the entire null hypothesis. When the number of bootstrap replications and the sample size diverge jointly at an appropriate rate, the test statistic, conditional on the data, is asymptotically pivotal. This implies that conditioning on this diagnostic does not induce pre-testing bias asymptotically. In simulations with Normal-inverse Gaussian shocks, the multivariate diagnostic is close to its nominal size under the null, its power against an additional Gaussian shock increases with the sample size, and its univariate version localizes the failure in large samples. Based on the estimates of a SVAR in the macroeconomic and financial uncertainty literature, we demonstrate its potential as a practical, robust tool for assessing non-Gaussian identification.
item.dc:creator: Paritosh Shankarrao Junare

item.title: Wrong Operator or Blind Design? A Post-Training Diagnostic for Physics-Informed Coefficient Learning
